source.title: DNN or k-NN: That is the Generalize vs. Memorize Question
source.authors: Gilad Cohen; G. Sapiro; R. Giryes

record.file_problem: Full text is present; it includes figures as captions but not their plotted values.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains a Wide-Resnet on randomized labels and reports training accuracy reaching 100%, directly testing random-label fitting.
record.gate_note: The randomized-label results are described in the text and Figures 4 and 6. The paper also cites Zhang et al. (2017); cited results are not included here. Figure-only accuracy values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study trains Wide-Resnet 28-10 on randomly labeled datasets and reports reaching 100% training accuracy, directly testing the random-label fitting component of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, the authors locate random-label memorization in the last layers and argue that memorization and generalization can coexist. They also report that DNN agreement with k-NN on learned representations accompanies good generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses randomized-label training and measures training accuracy, but its main analysis compares DNN predictions with classifiers fitted at network layers; details about keeping the original training hyperparameters unchanged are not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the randomized-label memorization pattern is confined to the last layers.

fits_no_version.finding: For random-label networks, memorization is localized to the last layers according to classifiers fitted to layer representations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-label memorization is concentrated in late network representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Training and test k-NN-to-DNN KL-divergence trends separate around attainment of perfect training accuracy on randomized datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Divergence between training and test classifier-agreement trends can indicate overfitting.

record.problems: The randomized-label results are largely presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The text does not specify whether the original architecture and training hyperparameters were unchanged, or report chance-level test error.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4 also presents train and test accuracies by layer for randomized counterparts, but its plotted values are not stated in the text; no separate rows were added beyond the explicit randomized training-accuracy result.

untested.parts: Numerical chance-level test performance, the precise random-label generation procedure, and unchanged training hyperparameters are not established by the supplied text. The same architecture is used for real and randomized datasets.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence as a function of corruption fraction.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test performance across intermediate label-corruption fractions.

Controlled effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization. The overfitting experiment jointly removes regularization and reduces training-set size.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels during training. Layer depth and classifier agreement do not establish this temporal ordering.

record.verdict_notes: The 100% result is supported by accompanying prose and captions, not merely by a definition of memorization. Figure 4's additional accuracy results are already declared in rows_left_out. No numerical optimization-time comparison can be recovered from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports randomized-label training accuracy reaching 100%, but does not establish chance test error or whether architecture and training hyperparameters were unchanged.

The paper removes data augmentation and weight decay while enforcing overfitting on real data, but does not test whether those methods prevent random-label fitting or whether their removal alone causes poor generalization.
